vignette:
In 2014, he is fifty-one years old, driving the last route of the night through the industrial edge of the city. The bus is nearly empty—just two passengers, a man and a woman, sitting apart. He notices nothing unusual until the man stands and walks forward, pulling a knife from his coat. The woman stays seated, watching. They force him off the route, into a vacant lot behind a shuttered factory. They make him kneel. For three days they keep him in a concrete room with no windows. They want money he does not have, and they take turns hurting him—burning his arms with a cigarette, forcing his head under rusty water, shocking him with wires from a car battery. He loses track of time. He prays. He hears them arguing. On the third morning they throw him out of a van onto a gravel road and drive away. He crawls to a gas station. Someone calls an ambulance.

Now he is sixty-one, still driving a bus. He has been married for thirty-seven years. His wife says he is not the same man, and he knows she is right. He wakes every night at 3:17, the exact time he remembers the first electric shock. In the dream it is always happening again—the concrete floor, the smell of diesel, the sound of the car battery humming. He lies still, afraid to move, until the alarm goes off at 4:45. His wife has stopped reaching for him. She sleeps on the far edge of the bed.

On the bus he scans every passenger who boards. He notices the hands first. Anyone holding a newspaper folded a certain way, or wearing a coat with deep pockets, makes his throat tighten. He avoids one particular stop—the warehouse district—even though it means a longer route and complaints from the dispatcher. Twice he has pulled over and asked a passenger to leave because the passenger’s voice reminded him of the man who held the wires. The company has written him up for erratic behavior. He tells himself he is just careful.

He cannot watch movies with violence. A sound effect of a scream on television sends him to the garage. His wife has stopped suggesting they watch anything together. She talks to him about bills, groceries, the neighbors. He nods but does not hear. He feels hollow, like the important part of him was left in that concrete room.

At work he operates the bus on autopilot—turns, stops, doors—while his mind drifts to the same scene. He counts the tiles in the warehouse ceiling in his head, over and over. Sometimes he catches himself gripping the steering wheel so hard his knuckles blanch. He has developed a habit of checking the rearview mirror every three or four seconds, even when the bus is empty. The other drivers joke that he is paranoid. He does not laugh.

He has not told his wife about the third day, when the men discussed whether to kill him. He has not told anyone. When a new driver asks about the scars on his forearms, he says he burned himself on a radiator. He avoids hospitals. He avoids the news. When the city council holds a ceremony for first responders, he calls in sick.

Mostly he feels tired. Not sleepy, but exhausted in a way that sleep does not fix. He does not look forward to anything. He does not remember the last time he felt happy. He thinks about the warehouse less than he used to, but the feeling of it—the cold, the helplessness—lives under his skin like a second language he cannot stop speaking.
